claim.markdown_says: ## D.19.3.3 Object data definitions   [while the immediately adjacent siblings are '### D.19.3.1 General', '### D.19.3.2 Object instantiations', '### D.19.3.4 Object references', '### D.19.3.5 Factory objects']
claim.why_it_matters: The heading is promoted one level, so D.19.3.3 renders as a peer of D.19.3 Objects instead of a child of it, breaking the document outline and any TOC/anchor tooling that walks heading depth. The same promotion recurs elsewhere in this batch: '## D.17.2 Intermediate rounding' (p1126) and '## D.17.3 Final rounding (the ROUNDED clause)' (p1127) against '### D.17.1 General'; '## D.18.2.2 Specification' and '## D.18.2.3 Examples' (p1131) against '### D.18.2.1 General'; '## D.18.3.2 Specification' and '## D.18.3.3 Examples' (p1133) against '### D.18.3.1 General'. In each group only the first '...N.1 General' child kept the correct depth and every later sibling was flattened up one level. No normative text is lost -- this is structural navigation only.

verdict.reasoning:
I attempted to refute this on four independent grounds and it survived all four.

(1) The markdown quote is accurate. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 45695 reads '## D.19.3.3 Object data definitions'. Its immediate siblings are line 45640 '### D.19.3.1 General', 45645 '### D.19.3.2 Object instantiations', 45731 '### D.19.3.4 Object references', 45754 '### D.19.3.5 Factory objects'. The parent at 45637 is '## D.19.3 Objects'. So D.19.3.3 sits at the same markdown depth as its own parent. Confirmed verbatim.

(2) The PDF quote is accurate, verified at the glyph/span level rather than by eye. Extracting the text-layer spans with PyMuPDF, every one of these headings is set in the identical face and size -- Cambria,Bold at 11.67 pt: D.19.3 and D.19.3.1 and D.19.3.2 (PDF index 1134), D.19.3.3 (PDF index 1135), D.19.3.4 and D.19.3.5 (PDF index 1136). The rendered page at 300 dpi agrees: 'D.19.3.3   Object data definitions' is printed in the same bold serif at the same size as the sibling headings on the facing pages. So the PDF's typography genuinely does not distinguish these levels, exactly as claimed.

(3) The decisive test, and the one I expected would refute the claim: since the PDF prints all clause headings at one uniform size, one could argue the markdown transcriber had no signal for depth and that heading level is therefore an arbitrary styling choice rather than a transcription fact. That defence fails, because the PDF carries its own embedded outline (2090 bookmark entries) and that outline encodes the hierarchy explicitly. In it, D.19.3 is level 3 and ALL FIVE of D.19.3.1, D.19.3.2, D.19.3.3, D.19.3.4, D.19.3.5 are level 4. The canonical source therefore states unambiguously that D.19.3.3 is a child of D.19.3 and a peer of the other four. The markdown contradicts a structural fact present in the PDF; this is not a stylistic preference.

(4) Not page-break furniture, wrapping, or hyphenation. The heading text itself is transcribed correctly and completely, and no body text is lost -- both code blocks and the intervening paragraph on p1136 match the print. I also chased the one apparent omission (the page's opening continuation clause 'uses the methods defined for the class to carry out its functions, for example, the deposit method credits the account.') and it is correctly merged into its parent paragraph at line 45663 in the p1135 slice. So the ONLY discrepancy on this page is the heading depth, and it is a real one.

Severity 'cosmetic' is fair -- zero normative content is affected -- but the structural blast radius is larger than the claim states (see corrected_description).
verdict.corrected_description:
REAL, but the described consequence is understated and the stated pattern is wrong for this group.

Understated consequence: promoting D.19.3.3 to '##' does not merely make it a peer of '## D.19.3 Objects'. Because the two headings that follow it are '### D.19.3.4' and '### D.19.3.5', those two are re-parented under D.19.3.3 in the rendered outline. The markdown outline therefore reads: '## D.19.3 Objects' with children .1 and .2; then '## D.19.3.3' with children .4 and .5. Three clauses are misplaced, not one, and any TOC walker sees D.19.3.4/.5 as grandchildren of D.19.3 via the wrong parent. The PDF outline puts all five at the same level under D.19.3.

Wrong generalization: the claim asserts 'In each group only the first ...N.1 General child kept the correct depth and every later sibling was flattened up one level.' That holds for the three cited comparison groups -- D.17 ('### D.17.1 General' vs '## D.17.2', '## D.17.3'), D.18.2 ('### D.18.2.1' vs '## D.18.2.2', '## D.18.2.3') and D.18.3 ('### D.18.3.1' vs '## D.18.3.2', '## D.18.3.3'), all confirmed in the file -- but it is false for the D.19.3 group that is actually on p1136. There, D.19.3.2, D.19.3.4 and D.19.3.5 all correctly kept '###'; D.19.3.3 is the lone outlier. The p1136 defect is an isolated one-heading promotion, not an instance of the 'everything after .1 got flattened' pattern.

Fix: change line 45695 of specs/ISO_COBOL.md from '## D.19.3.3 Object data definitions' to '### D.19.3.3 Object data definitions'.

Separate pre-existing defect noticed while verifying, NOT part of this claim and needing its own ledger entry: '## D.19.3 Objects' (line 45637) is itself promoted. The PDF outline puts D.19.3 at level 3, the same level as D.19.1 and D.19.2, which the markdown renders as '### D.19.1 General' and '### D.19.2 Classes'. So D.19.3 should be '###' and its children '####'. Repairing only line 45695 to '###' fixes the local sibling inconsistency and stops the re-parenting of .4/.5, but leaves the D.19.3-vs-D.19.1/.2 level mismatch in place.
